{"content":"This chapter introduces the fundamental concepts of lines and angles in geometry. A line segment has two endpoints, a ray has one endpoint, and a line extends infinitely in both directions. Points lying on the same line are called collinear points, while points not on the same line are non-collinear.

An angle is formed when two rays originate from a common vertex. Depending on their degree measurement, angles are classified into five main types: acute angles, right angles, obtuse angles, straight angles, and reflex angles. Complementary angles add up to 90 degrees, while supplementary angles sum to 180 degrees.

When two angles share a common vertex and arm, they are called adjacent angles. If the non-common arms form a straight line, the adjacent angles form a linear pair, and their sum is equal to 180 degrees. This principle is known as the Linear Pair Axiom.

Lines can be intersecting or parallel. When two straight lines intersect each other at a point, they create vertically opposite angles, which are equal. Furthermore, the sum of all angles formed around a single point is always 360 degrees. These fundamental rules and theorems form the foundation for solving geometric problems and understanding real-life applications.","filename":"summary_en.md"}
